manuscript-studio.name: Manuscript Studio
manuscript-studio.detail: Long worktables hold student experiment reports, revision notes, and stamped submissions.

east-glasshouse.name: East Glasshouse
east-glasshouse.detail: Humidity monitors blink beside sealed trays of rare silvermoss seedlings.

pattern-library.name: Pattern Library
pattern-library.detail: A shelf of language puzzles explains how an author can hide meaning in plain sight.

safety-office.name: Safety Office
safety-office.detail: Incident tickets, safety alerts, and response timestamps are filed here.

service-walk.name: Service Walk
service-walk.detail: Only authorized adults can access the ventilation mechanisms above the laboratory.

central-rotunda.name: Central Rotunda
central-rotunda.detail: Students trade theories beneath a projected schedule of academy presentations.

texts.1-2: Tavi wrote eight headings: Evidence, Air, Samples, Timing, Ventilation, Evaporation, Notes, Testing. Put their first letters together. The letters spell EAST VENT.
texts.3-5: Tavi Renn’s report GR-14 lists eight odd but meaningful headings in this order: Evidence, Air, Samples, Timing, Ventilation, Evaporation, Notes, Testing. Reading only the first letter of each heading gives E-A-S-T-V-E-N-T. A penciled note says, “Read the beginnings; they point to what needs attention.” It does not say that a student damaged anything.
texts.6-8: The signed original of experimental report GR-14 uses eight section headings—Evidence, Air, Samples, Timing, Ventilation, Evaporation, Notes, Testing. Their initials spell EASTVENT, an acrostic rather than an ordinary scientific term. An annotation in Tavi Renn’s handwriting states, “A reader who attends to beginnings will find the location the ordinary results cannot explain.” The content beneath each heading discusses legitimate observations; the unusual architecture of the report signals deliberate communication, not fabrication of measurements.

1-2.q: What do the first letters of the headings spell?
a: EAST VENT
WEST GATE
NEW BOOK
1-2.h: Read the first letter of each heading in order.
1-2.why: E-A-S-T-V-E-N-T spells EAST VENT, a place investigators should examine.

3-5.q: What is the most reasonable purpose of these unusual headings?
a: To hide the students’ names from the teacher
To point a careful reader toward the east vent
To describe eight different kinds of seeds
3-5.h: Put the first letters together before deciding what the headings mean.
3-5.why: The acrostic spells EAST VENT, making the headings a location clue rather than random labels.

6-8.q: Which interpretation best explains the report’s structure and authorship?
a: The eight initials prove the humidity data were invented
The headings came from an anonymous ancient prophecy
Tavi intentionally embedded an acrostic directing reviewers toward the east vent
6-8.h: Use the signed original, the first-letter pattern, and the author’s note together.
6-8.why: The signed report and explicit note support a purposeful location warning, not proof of data manipulation or a supernatural code.

texts.1-2: A desk book says Tavi turned in GR-14 at 8:24 on Monday. Milo checked the spelling later. Milo did not write the headings.
texts.3-5: The manuscript desk stamped Tavi Renn’s report GR-14 “received Monday, 8:24 a.m.” Its revision history shows Tavi added the eight headings at 8:21. Student editor Milo Quen reviewed punctuation at 8:42, but his revision did not change the headings. This record identifies the author and separates writing from later editing.
texts.6-8: The submission ledger assigns report GR-14 to Tavi Renn and preserves a revision diff: the acrostic headings entered at 8:21 a.m. and the finished version received at 8:24. Milo Quen’s later 8:42 editing pass changed two commas, leaving the heading sequence intact. As a timestamped record of document custody, the ledger is stronger evidence of authorship than Milo’s later description of an “odd poem,” though it does not by itself establish the warning’s meaning.

a: Milo Quen
Tavi Renn
Rowan Pike
1-2.h: Look for the writer named before the 8:24 stamp.
1-2.why: The ledger shows Tavi added the headings before Milo edited punctuation.

a: Milo edited commas at 8:42
Milo announced a rumor after class
Tavi added the headings at 8:21
3-5.h: Compare the timestamps in the revision history.
3-5.why: 8:21 comes before 8:24 and 8:42; Tavi wrote the coded headings before the report was submitted.

6-8.q: What can the revision trail establish more firmly than student gossip?
a: Tavi authored the coded headings before Milo’s later editing pass
Milo changed the ventilation setting at 8:42
The eight headings were automatically generated
6-8.h: Focus on time-stamped changes, not impressions about the report’s style.
6-8.why: The preserved revision diff attributes the deliberate wording to Tavi; authorship alone does not prove intent or sabotage.

texts.1-2: Lio wrote 5.2 on a sheet. The sensor really said 52. Lio crossed out 5.2 and wrote 52. It was a copying mistake.
texts.3-5: Student Lio Cale wrote “5.2 percent” beside a trial reading that actually showed “52 percent.” A red correction added before class explains the decimal point was copied in the wrong place. The reading concerns the west seed tray, not the east ventilation unit. Some students say every unusual number is part of the hidden message, but this one has a plain explanation.
texts.6-8: Lio Cale’s original data transcription shows a west-tray humidity reading entered as 5.2% and corrected to 52% after comparison with the instrument photograph. The correction bears a time and initials, and the unaffected trial labels match. Treating the decimal error as an intentional cipher confuses an independently documented clerical mistake with Tavi’s patterned headings. The two anomalies occurred in different records and served different functions.

a: Someone hid it in a poem
It was the room number
Its decimal point was put in the wrong place
1-2.h: Read the crossed-out number and the replacement.
1-2.why: Lio accidentally copied 52 as 5.2 and corrected it.

3-5.q: Why should detectives not treat every strange number as a code?
a: The sheet provides a documented copying error and its correction
Only long numbers can be clues
Students are never allowed to correct lab work
3-5.h: Compare the instrument photo with the original entry.
3-5.why: An identifiable transcription error is different from a deliberate repeated-letter pattern.

6-8.q: How does the decimal sheet sharpen the investigation’s distinction between accident and intention?
a: It demonstrates all student reports are unreliable
Its correction is corroborated by an instrument image, unlike the purposefully constructed acrostic
It proves Lio disabled the east vent
6-8.h: Consider whether independent evidence shows how the unusual entry arose.
6-8.why: The 5.2-to-52 change is explained by an ordinary copying mistake; patterned authorial choices in GR-14 require a different interpretation.

texts.1-2: The silvermoss needs wet air. The air was at 52 at 8:00 and fell to 29 at 8:10. The safe line is 40.
texts.3-5: A greenhouse chart shows the silvermoss trial area at 52% relative humidity at 8:00, 38% at 8:06, and 29% at 8:10. Staff had posted a minimum safe level of 40% for the seedlings. The sharp drop preceded Tavi’s report. The graph can show that something was wrong, but it cannot identify who changed the air system.
texts.6-8: The calibrated glasshouse logger records a rapid decline in relative humidity: 52% at 8:00, 38% at 8:06, and 29% at 8:10, below the 40% minimum defined by the silvermoss trial protocol. The graph establishes an environmental change before Tavi submitted GR-14. It neither identifies a deliberate actor nor distinguishes a stuck ventilation damper from alternative mechanical causes without inspection data.

1-2.q: Was the air too dry for silvermoss at 8:10?
a: Yes, it fell below 40
No, it was above 52
The chart shows no numbers
1-2.h: Find 29 and compare it with the safe line at 40.
1-2.why: At 8:10 humidity was 29%, below the required 40%.

3-5.q: Which event came before Tavi submitted the coded report?
a: The technician finished repairs
The greenhouse humidity dropped below its safe level
Milo announced the exhibit winner
3-5.h: Compare the 8:06–8:10 readings with the 8:24 report stamp.
3-5.why: The instrument recorded the moisture loss before Tavi wrote and submitted the report.

6-8.q: What is the strongest inference supported by the humidity chart alone?
a: Tavi deliberately opened a ventilation valve
The laboratory was already repaired by 8:06
An abnormal drying trend occurred before the coded warning, but the graph does not establish a culprit
6-8.h: Separate the observed pattern from guesses about how it arose.
6-8.why: The chart is reliable for the humidity trend, not for proving intent or identifying who caused the mechanical issue.

texts.1-2: At 8:12, Tavi told the safety office the plants were too dry. A receipt proves the office got the warning.
texts.3-5: A receipt shows that Tavi submitted a clear safety alert at 8:12 a.m.: “East glasshouse drying quickly; please inspect the ventilation.” Officer Farah Noll acknowledged it. The alert was routed as an ordinary request because the control panel incorrectly displayed “normal.” Tavi later placed a second, coded pointer in a report for the review team, not instead of reporting the problem.
texts.6-8: The safety system preserves Tavi’s signed 8:12 a.m. message describing rapid moisture loss and requesting immediate staff inspection of east-glasshouse ventilation. Farah Noll acknowledged receipt, but automated triage listed the task as routine because a separate damper-position indicator continued to read “normal.” The original alert is decisive context for author purpose: the subsequent acrostic reinforces a documented safety warning rather than secretly replacing approved reporting procedures.

1-2.q: Did Tavi tell an adult about the dry air?
a: No, Tavi kept it secret
Yes, Tavi sent a safety alert
Tavi sent only a joke
1-2.why: The signed message and receipt show Tavi reported the concern to the safety office.

3-5.q: Why is this safety alert important when judging the hidden message?
a: It proves Tavi wanted the plants to die
It shows the greenhouse was always dry
It shows Tavi had already used the official reporting process
3-5.h: Notice what Tavi reported before adding the acrostic.
3-5.why: Tavi explicitly sought an inspection before using the report as a backup signal.

6-8.q: Which reading best characterizes Tavi’s likely purpose when the acrostic is considered alongside this alert?
a: To reinforce a previously reported safety concern when the ticket was misprioritized
To circumvent all adult safety procedures with a secret contest
To accuse Milo publicly of forging scientific measurements
6-8.h: Compare the signed early alert with the later headings and the routing reason.
6-8.why: The contemporaneous request and subsequent acrostic align as two warnings about the same location, not evidence of sabotage or reckless secrecy.

texts.1-2: Rowan checked the east vent at 9:05. Its flap was stuck open. Dry air came in. Staff shut the flap safely.
texts.3-5: At 9:05 a.m., facilities technician Rowan Pike inspected ventilation unit EV-2 in the east glasshouse. Rowan found the damper stuck open while its display said “normal.” The official work order states that the open damper admitted dry air and explains the falling humidity. Authorized staff isolated the mechanism at 9:14 and moved the vulnerable seed trays. The finding confirms a mechanical fault, not a student prank.
texts.6-8: Inspection record EV-2, signed by authorized technician Rowan Pike at 9:05 a.m., identifies a jammed-open intake damper and a faulty position indicator that continued to signal “normal.” The uncontrolled intake explains the measured decline in humidity without positing intentional interference. At 9:14 the staff isolated the unit and transferred silvermoss trays to a stable cabinet. This independently produced technical record corroborates both the precise location encoded by Tavi and the environmental concern described in the safety alert.

1-2.q: What was wrong with the east vent?
a: A book was stuck inside it
The vent had no door
The vent flap was stuck open
1-2.why: The technician documented that the east vent damper was stuck open.

3-5.q: How does Rowan’s inspection help solve the mystery?
a: It confirms that the east vent had a mechanical problem
It proves Milo wrote GR-14
It reveals that Lio stole seedlings
3-5.h: Look for a checked fault rather than a witness guess.
3-5.why: The signed inspection independently verifies a stuck-open vent and explains the drying trend.

6-8.q: Why is this record essential corroboration for the acrostic?
a: It proves acrostics always describe malfunctioning machines
It provides an independently verified fault at the named location, connecting a coded pointer to a real safety hazard
It shows Tavi obtained unauthorized access to the damper
6-8.h: Ask what the record can prove that the heading letters alone cannot.
6-8.why: The acrostic supplies a location and the work order confirms the actual equipment fault and its environmental effect.

texts.1-2: Only adult helpers could open the service door. Rowan opened it at 9:02 to check the vent. Tavi did not enter.
texts.3-5: A door record lists service-gallery access only for trained staff. Rowan Pike used an authorized badge at 9:02 a.m. for inspection. Tavi’s student badge never opened that door. The log rules out rumors that the message’s author slipped inside to change the vent; it does not tell the detectives who composed the report.
texts.6-8: The electronic service-access audit records Rowan’s authorized entry at 9:02 and no student badge activity in the ventilation gallery that morning. Because the control equipment is restricted, these records undercut claims that Tavi clandestinely altered the east damper. However, absence of an access log entry alone does not prove a particular person wrote the acrostic; authorship must be established using the report provenance.

1-2.q: Who was allowed into the service area?
a: Trained adult staff
Every student
Only library visitors
1-2.why: The schedule restricts access to authorized adults like Rowan.

3-5.q: Which rumor does the service log weaken?
a: That the report had eight headings
That Tavi entered the service gallery to tamper with the vent
That Milo fixed punctuation later
3-5.h: Check whether any student badge opened the door.
3-5.why: No student badge entered the restricted gallery, so a student-tampering claim lacks supporting access evidence.

6-8.q: What is the most careful use of this negative evidence?
a: It establishes that the damper could not malfunction
It proves Rowan intentionally broke the ventilation unit
It weakens a claim of unauthorized student access but does not identify the message author
6-8.h: Remember what the log does and does not measure.
6-8.why: An absence of student access is relevant to sabotage allegations, but it does not independently settle authorship or explain the damper jam.

texts.1-2: A poster says, “A student changed the air machine!” It has no name and no proof. People keep repeating it.
texts.3-5: An unsigned poster displayed at 8:48 a.m. declares, “SECRET CODE MEANS STUDENT SABOTAGE!” It quotes the word “vent” but cites no original document or access record. The anonymous claim spread after Milo pointed out unusual headings. Its dramatic language may attract attention, but it is weaker than the signed report and official maintenance findings.
texts.6-8: An anonymous rotunda poster claims an encoded report “confesses to sabotaging ventilation.” Its author cites neither direct observation nor a credible document and omits the earlier safety alert. The poster is an interpretation—secondary commentary shaped to provoke suspicion—not primary evidence of who touched the machinery. Evaluating its purpose and omissions is essential before accepting a sensational conclusion.

1-2.q: Does the poster prove anyone broke the vent?
a: Yes, posters are always correct
No, it gives no evidence
Yes, it has a bright title
1-2.h: Look for a signer or a record named as proof.
1-2.why: The unsigned poster makes an accusation without providing firsthand evidence.

3-5.q: Why should detectives treat the poster cautiously?
a: It appears in a public hallway
It uses capital letters instead of lowercase
It makes a strong claim without citing reliable evidence
3-5.h: Find whether the claim includes a source or direct observation.
3-5.why: The poster is a rumor and does not establish sabotage.

6-8.q: Which flaw most weakens the poster as a source?
a: It substitutes an unsupported interpretation for evidence and omits a contrary official alert
It contains the word “vent” rather than “damper”
It was posted before lunchtime instead of afterward
6-8.h: Evaluate authorship, corroboration, and selective omission.
6-8.why: Without provenance or supporting records, the claim is less credible than the signed alert, audit, and inspection.

texts.1-2: A book explains an acrostic. Read the first letter of each line to find a word. Not all odd words are codes.
texts.3-5: The language library defines an acrostic as a message made from the first letters of lines or headings. A practice example spells SUN from “Shade, Under, Night.” The librarian’s notes caution that a real code has an intentional, repeatable pattern; an accidental spelling mistake usually does not. The book explains how to test GR-14 without assuming every error is secret.
texts.6-8: The library’s annotated wordplay manual distinguishes acrostic encoding from mere irregularity. An acrostic uses a deliberately controlled initial-letter sequence that yields a meaningful phrase when read in order. Its practice example produces SUN from three headings. The manual is a secondary reference about technique, not direct testimony about the academy incident, and therefore it can help decode GR-14 but cannot identify the author on its own.

1-2.q: Where do you look for an acrostic message?
a: Only at the last page
Only in numbers
At the first letters of lines or headings
1-2.h: Read the example with S, U, and N.
1-2.why: An acrostic is made by reading initial letters in sequence.

3-5.q: How does the library book help with GR-14?
a: It teaches a method for testing a meaningful first-letter pattern
It proves all typing mistakes are codes
It names the person who damaged the vent
3-5.h: Apply the definition to the unusual headings.
3-5.why: The reference explains how EASTVENT can emerge from initial letters without proving the underlying incident.

6-8.q: What is the best assessment of this source’s evidentiary role?
a: It is firsthand testimony from the technician
It explains the encoding method but cannot independently establish who wrote the report or why
It proves intentional wrongdoing whenever initials form a word
6-8.h: Distinguish a general reference work from an original record of the specific event.
6-8.why: The reference supports the decoding technique; the submission ledger and safety records establish authorship and purpose.

texts.1-2: Silvermoss grows in damp air. Below 40, staff must move the seed trays to a safe cabinet. Staff moved them at 9:14.
texts.3-5: The silvermoss care card requires relative humidity above 40% for the study and instructs trained staff to move trays to the stable cabinet if the value stays below the limit. A follow-up note says the seedlings were moved at 9:14 a.m. The care card explains why a ventilation problem matters to the experiment, not only to the building.
texts.6-8: The trial protocol establishes an environmental threshold of 40% relative humidity and calls for authorized staff relocation of trays if the threshold is breached. A signed transfer addendum at 9:14 records that specimens were moved to a controlled cabinet without loss. The protocol clarifies the stakes of Tavi’s communication: preservation of living research materials. It does not imply the reporter caused the hazard.

1-2.q: Why did staff move the silvermoss trays?
a: The air was too dry for them
The class wanted more desk space
The trays were made of gold
1-2.h: Find the rule about humidity below 40.
1-2.why: The care protocol called for moving seedlings when air became too dry.

3-5.q: What does the care protocol explain about the report’s warning?
a: It proves the museum needed new shelves
The dry-air problem threatened the seedlings, so the location mattered
It requires students to open the service panel
3-5.h: Read the temperature and moisture rule, then connect it to the chart.
3-5.why: The seedlings needed protection, giving a practical reason for highlighting a failing vent.

6-8.q: Which theme emerges when this protocol is compared with Tavi’s warning?
a: Hidden messages are always more reliable than official safety systems
Scientific discoveries must be kept secret from adults
Careful communication can protect shared research when readers confirm claims with evidence
6-8.h: Connect the rule, the early alert, and the later authorized response.
6-8.why: Tavi’s paired direct and coded warnings encouraged attentive review; the authorized response protected research materials.

texts.1-2: “I saw the dry air,” says Tavi. “I told the safety office. I also put EAST VENT in my report headings so readers would check it.”
texts.3-5: Tavi says, “When the humidity dropped, I alerted the safety office at 8:12. The ticket was marked routine even though I worried about the seedlings. I added the first letters EAST VENT to GR-14 so reviewers would notice exactly where to look. I did not open the service door.” Tavi’s account matches the signed alert and revision log, but detectives should confirm those records.
texts.6-8: Tavi Renn acknowledges deliberate authorship of GR-14’s acrostic: “I wanted reviewers to connect the drying trend with the east intake. I had already filed a direct alert, but the control panel still read normal and the routing marked it routine. The patterned headings were a second way of attracting careful attention, not a substitute for the safety process.” Tavi denies entering the restricted gallery, a claim supported by access logs; still, the interview should be evaluated alongside contemporaneous documents.

1-2.q: Why did Tavi use first letters?
a: To trick a spelling contest
To tell readers to check the east vent
To hide a treasure map
1-2.h: Listen for what Tavi wanted readers to check.
1-2.why: Tavi says the headings were a backup warning about EAST VENT.

3-5.q: What is the most supported interpretation of Tavi’s motive?
a: Tavi wanted credit for damaging school property
Tavi wanted to replace all lab instructions with riddles
Tavi wanted the review team to notice the location of an already reported problem
3-5.h: Compare Tavi’s explanation with the time-stamped safety alert.
3-5.why: The earlier official report corroborates Tavi’s stated purpose of reinforcing a legitimate warning.

6-8.q: Which combination most responsibly evaluates Tavi’s reliability?
a: Check the author’s claim against the 8:12 signed alert, revision trail, and restricted-access audit
Accept every statement because Tavi seems sincere
Dismiss the testimony because the writing uses wordplay
6-8.h: Choose corroborating records created before or independently of the interview.
6-8.why: Multiple contemporaneous records corroborate authorship and prior reporting, while the access audit weakens accusations of tampering.

texts.1-2: “I saw strange headings and thought they were a poem,” says Milo. “I fixed commas. I did not write the headings.”
texts.3-5: Milo says, “The report looked like a language puzzle, so I called it a secret poem. I edited two commas after Tavi turned it in. I never meant to start a rumor that it proved cheating.” Milo admits that his first reading focused on style, not the humidity data. The revision ledger lets detectives check which words he actually changed.
texts.6-8: Milo Quen describes his initial genre assumption: “Because we study rhetoric here, I treated the headings as a literary flourish rather than a technical pointer.” He acknowledges sharing that impression, which others exaggerated into an accusation of sabotage. A subsequent revision diff limits Milo’s role to comma edits. His interview reveals how a plausible but unsupported interpretation can spread when a reader neglects a document’s broader context.

1-2.q: What did Milo change in the report?
a: All eight headings
The air vent
Two commas
1-2.h: Look for the small edits Milo names.
1-2.why: Milo edited punctuation and did not create the coded headings.

3-5.q: What was Milo’s first mistake as a reader?
a: He judged the headings as creative style without checking the data and context
He measured the humidity too carefully
He refused to read any report
3-5.h: Compare his first assumption with the scientific clues.
3-5.why: Milo’s stylistic interpretation overlooked that the acrostic pointed toward a real equipment problem.

6-8.q: What broader reading lesson does Milo’s interview illustrate?
a: Every creative heading must be a false statement
An initial interpretation can be biased by expectations about genre and should be revised using context
A copy editor automatically becomes the original author
6-8.h: Notice why Milo expected a poem rather than a warning.
6-8.why: Milo’s expectation of wordplay shaped his reading; the instrument records and authorship ledger justify revising it.

texts.1-2: “I wrote 5.2 but meant 52,” says Lio. “I fixed it. That mistake was not the secret code.”
texts.3-5: Lio says, “The west-tray sensor showed 52%, but I added a decimal when I copied it. We compared the sensor photo and corrected my sheet before class.” Lio admits being embarrassed when students suggested the number was a cipher. The correction has nothing to do with the east-vent fault, though both documents teach investigators to read carefully.
texts.6-8: Lio Cale concedes a transcription error involving a decimal point in a west-tray reading and directs investigators to a timestamped image of the instrument. Lio distinguishes unintentional numerical error from Tavi’s repeated intentional choices in language. The confession is credible because the original photo and signed correction corroborate it; embarrassment alone neither proves nor refutes involvement in the ventilation incident.

1-2.q: Was Lio’s number mistake a planned message?
a: No, it was an ordinary copying error
Yes, it spelled EAST
Yes, it was a secret door code
1-2.h: Lio explains how the decimal got misplaced.
1-2.why: The sensor photo confirms that Lio accidentally wrote the wrong number.

3-5.q: What should a detective do with Lio’s explanation?
a: Assume Lio wrote the acrostic too
Check it against the original sensor photo and correction
Ignore the correction because it is embarrassing
3-5.h: Look for independent evidence of the number before it was copied.
3-5.why: The instrument image and corrected worksheet support an accidental error rather than a code.

6-8.q: What contrast between Lio’s sheet and Tavi’s report is best supported?
a: Both were necessarily invented to hide the same problem
Neither document can be understood without guessing
The number has an independently verified copying cause; the patterned headings and author note indicate intention
6-8.h: Compare provenance and the regularity of the anomalous patterns.
6-8.why: The decimal slip is mechanically explainable; the coherent first-letter phrase and author annotation indicate deliberate message design.

texts.1-2: “I got Tavi’s note at 8:12,” says Farah. “The screen said the vent was normal, but I asked Rowan to check it.”
texts.3-5: Farah says, “I acknowledged Tavi’s alert at 8:12. Our ticket list displayed it as routine because the damper’s position sensor still showed normal. As the humidity report grew worse, I requested an inspection. Students were not allowed to handle the machinery.” Farah’s statement explains a delay without claiming an intentional cover-up.
texts.6-8: Safety officer Farah Noll confirms the direct alert entered the approved channel at 8:12 but initially received a routine priority because a faulty position indicator contradicted the humidity readings. She escalated the concern for technician inspection and explicitly restricted students from the service gallery. Her testimony distinguishes an imperfect response system from deliberate concealment; the ticket and work order allow the chronology to be verified independently.

a: Milo in the library
Farah in the safety office
A visitor at the gate
1-2.h: Find Farah’s job and the time she names.
1-2.why: Farah says she received Tavi’s 8:12 safety warning.

3-5.q: Why was the first safety ticket not treated as urgent?
a: The seedlings needed no moisture
Farah had never seen a report before
A faulty panel still displayed the vent as normal
3-5.h: Look for the disagreement between the humidity readings and the damper indicator.
3-5.why: The misleading normal-status display caused the ticket to be routed routinely until staff escalated it.

6-8.q: What nuanced inference about institutional response is supported by Farah’s account?
a: Staff received the report, but misleading sensor information delayed prioritization; the response was not shown to be malicious
Staff ordered Tavi to falsify the report
The school forbade safety reports that included numbers
6-8.h: Separate documented procedural delay from claims of intent.
6-8.why: The verified false-normal indicator explains the routing error without evidence of a cover-up or deliberate damage.

texts.1-2: “I checked the east vent,” says Rowan. “A flap stuck open. We closed it and kept the seedlings safe.”
texts.3-5: Rowan says, “At 9:05 I examined unit EV-2 and found its intake damper stuck open while the panel said normal. It kept pulling dry air into the silvermoss room. I isolated the unit at 9:14 while staff moved the seed trays.” Rowan denies finding tool marks or signs of student interference. The signed inspection lists the same findings.
texts.6-8: Rowan Pike’s technical assessment identifies a jammed-open damper in east-glasshouse unit EV-2 and a position sensor that falsely indicated closure. Rowan observed no fresh tampering marks, documented the fault in a signed 9:05 inspection, and oversaw safe isolation at 9:14. The technician stresses that the evidence supports equipment failure and urgent protective action, not an attribution of blame to whichever student drew attention to it.

1-2.q: What did Rowan find at the east vent?
a: A locked bookcase
A missing trophy
A stuck-open flap
1-2.h: Look for the part Rowan inspected.
1-2.why: Rowan found a ventilation flap that would not close.

3-5.q: Which claim does Rowan’s signed report most directly support?
a: Dry air entered because the east vent damper was stuck open
Tavi changed the report after 9:14
Milo broke a lock to get to the vent
3-5.h: Compare the signed finding with the rumor poster.
3-5.why: The official inspection connects the environmental problem to an equipment fault, not a student plot.

6-8.q: How does Rowan’s testimony change the strongest explanation of the mystery?
a: It proves that every student who used figurative language was lying
It independently links the acrostic’s destination to a genuine mechanical fault and undercuts sabotage claims
It makes the humidity data irrelevant
6-8.h: Identify what the technician observed directly and documented.
6-8.why: A documented jammed damper explains the drying pattern and corroborates the location Tavi encoded in GR-14.

case.title: The Secret Academy
case.subtitle: CASE FILE 013 • READ BETWEEN THE HEADINGS
case.goal: Find who hid a purposeful warning in a student experiment report, which place the code identified, and why it was written. Distinguish a harmless copying error from a meaningful pattern; use documentary proof rather than rumors.

brief.1-2: At Emberrise Academy, someone wrote a hidden message in a science report! A greenhouse is too dry for silvermoss plants. Read first letters, ask questions, and find who wrote the warning, where it points, and why the writer wanted help.
brief.3-5: Emberrise Academy teaches science and language together. During a silvermoss experiment, greenhouse humidity drops sharply. Eight unusual headings appear in report GR-14, and students argue whether they reveal a secret prank, a cheating scheme, or an urgent clue. One student also makes an ordinary decimal error that spreads confusion. Compare the original report, timestamps, lab readings, safety alert, and witness accounts to decide who wrote the encoded message, where it points, and what the writer intended.
brief.6-8: At Emberrise Academy, a fictional institution where students learn field science alongside close reading, experiment report GR-14 contains a deliberate first-letter pattern hidden in otherwise legitimate section headings. Its circulation coincides with an abrupt drop in greenhouse humidity, a disputed clerical correction, and an unsigned accusation of sabotage. Competing interpretations grow as students mistake genre conventions, transcription errors, and purposeful encoding for the same kind of anomaly. Trace the authorship of the report, distinguish eyewitness observations from secondary claims, evaluate how institutional routing affected an earlier safety alert, and determine the intended audience and purpose of the code before submitting your evidence-backed final theory.

feedback.who: Check the signed SUBMISSION AND REVISION LEDGER against the original EIGHT-HEADING REPORT. Tavi created the initial-letter pattern at 8:21 and submitted the report at 8:24. Milo only edited commas later; Lio corrected a decimal; the adults responded to the report rather than writing it.
feedback.where: Use the PATTERN LIBRARY primer to read the first letter of each GR-14 heading: E-A-S-T-V-E-N-T. Then check Rowan’s signed INSPECTION EV-2. The west-tray decimal error and rotunda poster do not name the ventilation fault identified by the code.
feedback.why: Look at the order of events. At 8:12 Tavi filed a DIRECT SAFETY ALERT about drying seedlings; at 8:21 the coded headings were written, and the 9:05 inspection confirmed a fault. The evidence supports a backup warning to reviewers, not secret tampering, cheating, or a prank.
feedback.proofs: Choose BOTH the signed EIGHT-HEADING REPORT GR-14 (the authored coded message itself) AND ROWAN’S EV-2 INSPECTION RECORD (independent confirmation of the jammed-open east vent). The safety alert and submission ledger are useful supporting context, but alone they do not show both the code’s location and the real mechanical problem.

resolution.summary: Tavi Renn intentionally encoded EAST VENT in the headings of report GR-14 to reinforce a safety alert about drying silvermoss seedlings. Authorized staff confirmed a stuck-open damper in east glasshouse unit EV-2; there was no sabotage.
resolution.outcome: The secret message was a warning, not a confession or a student prank. On Monday at 8:00 a.m., Emberrise Academy’s silvermoss trial area was at 52% relative humidity. By 8:10 it had fallen to 29%, far below the trial’s 40% minimum. Student report author Tavi Renn noticed the pattern and responsibly sent an explicit safety alert at 8:12; safety officer Farah Noll received it. Unfortunately, the damper-position indicator still showed “normal,” so the ticket was initially classed as routine. Concerned that reviewers might miss the link between the humidity figures and the affected area, Tavi added eight meaningful section headings to experiment report GR-14 at 8:21: Evidence, Air, Samples, Timing, Ventilation, Evaporation, Notes, Testing. The headings’ first letters spell EASTVENT, a deliberate backup pointer to the east glasshouse ventilation. Tavi submitted the report at 8:24, and manuscript editor Milo Quen only corrected commas later; Milo did not invent the message. Meanwhile Lio Cale’s unrelated 5.2-versus-52 decimal correction created another puzzle that some students mistakenly treated as a code. A sensational unsigned poster then turned speculation into a claim of sabotage, but it cited no firsthand evidence. At 9:02 trained technician Rowan Pike entered the restricted service gallery and, by 9:05, documented east ventilation unit EV-2’s intake damper stuck open with a faulty normal-status indicator. The real malfunction caused the drying. No access record or inspection finding supported student interference. At 9:14 staff isolated the unit and moved the silvermoss trays into stable storage, preventing loss of the experiment. The signed original coded report shows exactly where Tavi directed attention; Rowan’s independent inspection explains why the warning mattered. The academy revised ticket-routing practice and reminded students to report safety concerns openly first while using careful writing to communicate evidence clearly. Investigators learned that an unusual mark is not always a cipher, that a cipher is not automatically malicious, and that understanding author purpose requires reading the entire chain of sources.

timeline.event: The silvermoss trial area records 52% humidity; the trial requires at least 40%.
Humidity drops below the safe minimum, registering 38% as dry air enters the east glasshouse.
The logger records 29%; Tavi checks the trend and recognizes the urgency.
Tavi submits a direct safety alert; Farah acknowledges receipt, but the vent indicator still misleadingly reads normal.
The safety system routes the alert as routine while Farah starts reviewing the conflicting readings.
Tavi creates eight GR-14 headings whose initials spell EASTVENT, reinforcing the earlier explicit warning.
Tavi submits the report; the manuscript ledger records original authorship and timestamp.
Milo changes two commas but leaves the heading sequence intact; his “secret poem” remark begins circulating.
An unsigned hallway poster wrongly claims that a secret code proves a student sabotaged the ventilation.
Rowan uses authorized access to enter the restricted service walkway.
Rowan documents EV-2’s jammed-open east damper and faulty normal-status sensor in a signed inspection report.
Authorized staff isolate the vent and transfer silvermoss trays to a stable cabinet; the rumor is corrected and the case closes.
